prompt: What is a callback?

choices.text: A function that calls itself
choices.why: That is recursion.

choices.text: A function passed in to be called later
choices.why: Right. Every function given to `map` was one.

choices.text: A function that returns another function
choices.why: That is one kind of higher-order function.

choices.text: Any function declared with `function` instead of `=>`
choices.why: Either syntax can be a callback.

prompt: `const say = shout;` How many functions exist after that line?

choices.text: One, with two names
choices.why: Right. The reference was copied.

choices.text: Two, since `say` is a copy of `shout`
choices.why: Assignment never copies an object, and a function is one.

choices.text: None: the line calls `shout` and stores the result
choices.why: There are no parentheses, so nothing is called.

choices.text: One, and `shout` is no longer usable
choices.why: Both names still work.

prompt: Match each property of `function shout(text)` with its value.
`hello` and `ola` came from `makeGreeting`, and each remembered a different greeting. Where was each greeting kept?
hint: Each call of `makeGreeting` has its own `greeting`.

choices.text: In a global variable that each call overwrites
choices.why: Then both would say the last greeting.

choices.text: Inside the string returned by `makeGreeting`
choices.why: `makeGreeting` returns a function, not a string.

choices.text: In the scope of the call that created it
choices.why: Right, and the next sections give that a name.

choices.text: In `makeGreeting.length`
choices.why: `length` is the number of parameters.

prompt: In what order does `describeBook` look for `library`?

choices.text: The file first, then `openShelf`, then its own scope
choices.why: That is outside in; the lookup goes inside out.

choices.text: Its own scope, then `openShelf`, then the file
choices.why: Right: it stops at the first scope that has the name.

choices.text: Whichever function called it, then the file
choices.why: The chain follows where the code is written, not who calls it.

choices.text: Only its own scope, then it gives up
choices.why: It found `library`, which was not in its own scope.

prompt: Why is this kind of scope called lexical?
hint: Can you work it out without running the code?

choices.text: Because it is decided when the function is called
choices.why: That describes `this`, not scope.

choices.text: Because names are sorted alphabetically
choices.why: Order of lookup is by nesting, not by spelling.

choices.text: It follows where the code is written
choices.why: Right, so reading the source tells you.

choices.text: Because only `let` and `const` follow it
choices.why: Every declaration follows the scope chain.

prompt: Can `openShelf` read the `title` parameter of `describeBook`?

choices.text: Yes, once `describeBook` has been called
choices.why: Calling it does not change the direction of lookups.

choices.text: No: `title` is in a scope inside it
choices.why: Right. Lookups go outwards only.

choices.text: Yes, because `describeBook` is written inside `openShelf`
choices.why: That gives `describeBook` access to `openShelf`'s names, not the reverse.

choices.text: Only if `title` is declared with `var`
choices.why: A parameter belongs to its function whatever the keyword.

prompt: The sequence of scopes a name is looked up through, from inside out, is called the scope ___.
hint: One word, like links joined end to end.

prompt: `visits(), visits(), visits()` printed `1 2 3`, then `loans()` printed `1`. Why did `loans` start at 1?

choices.text: Each call to `loans` resets every counter
choices.why: `visits` carried on to 4 afterwards.

choices.text: Counters start again after three calls
choices.why: Nothing in the code counts to three.

choices.text: Its own `count`, from its own call
choices.why: Right. Two calls, two scopes.

choices.text: `loans` is a copy of `visits` made before the calls
choices.why: They are two different functions from two calls.

prompt: `let message = "first"; const read = () => message; message = "changed later";` What does `read()` return now?

choices.text: `"first"`, the value when `read` was written
choices.why: That would be a copy; a closure keeps the variable.

choices.text: `"changed later"`
choices.why: Right. It sees every later change.

choices.text: `undefined`, because `message` was reassigned
choices.why: Reassigning gives it a new value, which `read` sees.

choices.text: A `TypeError` for changing a captured variable
choices.why: Captured variables can change like any other.

prompt: `typeof count` printed `undefined` at the end of `counter.js`. What does that show?

choices.text: `count` is reachable only through the functions that closed over it
choices.why: Right. That is the privacy the next section uses.

choices.text: `count` was deleted when `makeCounter` returned
choices.why: `visits()` kept counting, so it was still there.

choices.text: `typeof` does not work on numbers
choices.why: `typeof 4` is `"number"`.

choices.text: `count` was declared with `let`, which hides it from `typeof`
choices.why: The keyword is not why; the scope is.

prompt: A function together with the scope it was created in is called a ___.
hint: The word in the lesson's title.

prompt: `connect` was called three times. How many times did `connecting...` print?

choices.text: Three, once per call
choices.why: The wrapped function runs only on the first call.

choices.text: Once, on the first call
choices.why: Right. Later calls return the remembered result.

choices.text: Twice, since the first call only sets `done`
choices.why: The first call sets `done` and runs `fn`.

choices.text: Never, since `once` returns before calling it
choices.why: The returned arrow calls `fn` the first time it runs.

prompt: `square(12), square(12), square(5), square(12)` ran through `memoize`. How many times did `slowSquare` actually run?
After `acc.balanceCents = 1000000`, `acc.balance()` still said 1990. Why?
hint: Where does the real balance live?

choices.text: The assignment was refused with an error
choices.why: There was no error; it created a property.

choices.text: `balance()` caches its first answer
choices.why: It reads the variable each time.

choices.text: Numbers above a million are ignored
choices.why: The size of the number has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: It created an unrelated property; the balance lives in the closure
choices.why: Right. Only `deposit` can change it.

prompt: Which function is worth memoizing, by the section's rule?
hint: Slow, and the same answer for the same input.

choices.text: One that returns the current time
choices.why: Its answer changes on every call, so a cache would serve stale times.

choices.text: A slow calculation of a book's reading level from its text
choices.why: Right: slow, and the same text gives the same level.

choices.text: One that returns a random number
choices.why: A cached random number is not random.

choices.text: One that adds two small numbers
choices.why: It is already fast; the cache would cost more than it saves.

prompt: In `book.describe()`, what is `this` inside `describe`?

choices.text: `book`
choices.why: Right. It printed `true` for `=== book`.

choices.text: The function `describe`
choices.why: `this` is not the function itself.

choices.text: The global object
choices.why: That is a plain call in sloppy mode.

choices.text: `undefined`
choices.why: That is a plain call in strict mode.

prompt: Match each way of calling with the `this` it gives, in strict mode.
What decides the value of `this` in a normal function?
hint: The opposite of the rule for every other name.

choices.text: Where the function is written
choices.why: That is the rule for scope, and for arrows.

choices.text: The first object the function was assigned to
choices.why: A function belongs to no object.

choices.text: How it is called
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The file it is in
choices.why: The file does not decide `this` for a normal function.

prompt: Why did the arrow at the top of `this-rules.js` print `{}`?
hint: An arrow uses the `this` around it.

choices.text: Arrows always return an empty object for `this`
choices.why: An arrow inside a method gets the method's `this`, as `withArrow` showed.

choices.text: `"use strict"` turns `this` into `{}`
choices.why: Strict mode gives `undefined` for a plain call.

choices.text: At a Node file's top level, `this` is the module's exports, an empty object
choices.why: Right, and lesson 9 explains where that comes from.

choices.text: It printed the arrow function itself
choices.why: A function would print as `[Function: arrow]`.

prompt: `const label = shelf.label; label("Iracema");` threw. Why?
hint: Is there a dot in the call?

choices.text: `label` is a reserved name
choices.why: It is an ordinary name.

choices.text: Called with no dot, `this` was `undefined`
choices.why: Right: strict mode, plain call.

choices.text: The assignment copied the method without its body
choices.why: The whole function was referenced; the error came from inside its body.

choices.text: `shelf.prefix` was deleted by the assignment
choices.why: `shelf` was untouched.

prompt: `titles.map(shelf.label)` loses `this`. Which of these fix it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `titles.map((t) => shelf.label(t))`
choices.why: Yes: the call keeps its dot.

choices.text: Binding the method to `shelf` first (lesson 7)
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: `titles.map(shelf.label())`
choices.why: That calls `label` once, with no title, and passes its result to `map`.

choices.text: Defining `label` as an arrow-function class field (lesson 8)
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Removing `"use strict"`
choices.why: `this` becomes the global object, which has no `prefix`: a wrong answer instead of an error.

prompt: In `withFunction`, why did each line say `undefined:` instead of `Classics:`?

choices.text: `map` cannot be used inside a method
choices.why: `withArrow` used it in the same place and worked.

choices.text: `this.name` is a reserved property
choices.why: `name` is ordinary on `shelf`.

choices.text: `this.titles` was empty
choices.why: Two titles were printed.

choices.text: `map` called the inner function without an object, so it got its own `this`
choices.why: Right; an arrow would have used the method's.

prompt: A class's method is passed to `setTimeout` and later throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`. What is the cause, most directly?
hint: Classes are strict, and the method left its dot behind.

choices.text: `setTimeout` deletes the object before running the callback
choices.why: Nothing deletes the object.

choices.text: It was called with no object in front, leaving `this` unset
choices.why: Right. Wrap it in an arrow, bind it, or make it an arrow field.

choices.text: Timers cannot call methods, only plain functions
choices.why: A method is a function; the problem is the missing object.

choices.text: The closure lost its variables after the delay
choices.why: A closure keeps its variables for as long as the function exists.

prompt: Put the lookup of a name used inside `describeBook` in order.
trap: The function that called `describeBook` is not on the list: the chain follows where code is written.
